extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying, making, avoiding, and overcoming statutory and nonstatutory double patenting rejections during patent examination, including use of form paragraphs, terminal disclaimers, and statutory exceptions (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 121 and 103(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstatutory double patenting principle (prevent timewise extension)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental reason for the rule is to prevent unjustified timewise extension of the right to exclude granted by a patent no matter how the extension is brought about; appellant has the burden of establishing that the invention claimed in his patent is 'independent and distinct' from the invention of the appealed claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Schneller: even if ABCX and ABCY are technically different, allowance that extends patent protection for subject matter covered by an earlier patent must be prevented unless independent and distinctness is established. Nonstatutory double patenting rejections based on Schneller will be rare and are limited to the particular facts of that case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approval process for Schneller-based nonstatutory double patenting rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonstatutory double patenting rejections based on In re Schneller require Technology Center (TC) Director approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an examiner determines such a rejection is appropriate, consult the supervisory patent examiner (SPE); if the SPE agrees, obtain TC Director approval before making the rejection. Form paragraph usage is limited to situations where TC Director approval has been obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-specific nature and rarity of Schneller rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: In re Schneller did not establish a rule of general application and is limited to its particular set of facts; nonstatutory double patenting rejections based on Schneller will be rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid generalizing Schneller beyond its facts; treat similar situations cautiously and seek higher-level approval (TC Director) before applying Schneller-based rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of form paragraphs for nonstatutory double patenting rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph 8.33 and the appropriate one of form paragraphs 8.38 (with a patent) and 8.39 (provisional rejections with another application) may be used to make nonstatutory double patenting rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ¶8.38 (with a patent): insert patent number and describe common subject matter; use only where TC Director approval (for Schneller-based) obtained; use only when subject matter fully disclosed in and covered by at least one claim of an issued U.S. patent which is commonly owned or where there is common inventorship. Examiner notes (1-7) supply conditions and cross-references (e.g., use of form paragraph 7.21 when 102/103 issues arise). ¶8.39 (with copending application): similar bracket insertion rules and examiner notes; provisional rejection because conflicting claims have not been patented. Form paragraph 8.33 must precede 8.34–8.39 and be used only once in an Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kaplan: treatment of broad vs. narrow claims and joint inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere domination of a narrower claim by a broader patent claim does not per se justify a double patenting rejection; the disclosure of a joint invention in a patent cannot be treated as though it were prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider inventorship and why narrower claims were not presented in the earlier patent (e.g., statutory reasons precluding joint inventorship filings prior to 1984). Don't improperly use the patent specification's disclosure as prior art in double patenting analysis; analyze reasons for separate filings and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-by-case analysis requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Each double patenting situation must be decided on its own facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid blanket application; evaluate factual circumstances such as disclosure overlap, inventorship, filing timing, and statutory context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of double patenting to design and plant situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Double patenting principles applied in utility-utility situations generally apply to utility-plant and utility-design situations; rejection may be made where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design-utility cases may require a two-way obviousness determination; examine whether claims involve the same invention or obvious variations. Review cited case law (Carman, Thorington, Phelan, Barber, Hargraves) for precedential guidance and consider differences in claimed subject matter (external appearance vs interior construction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between double patenting and prior art rejections (35 U.S.C. 102/103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A double patenting rejection must rely on a comparison with the claims in an issued or to-be-issued patent, whereas a 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103(a) rejection relies on what is disclosed in the reference (claimed or unclaimed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In 102(e)/103(a) rejections, the reference patent is available for all that it fairly discloses; a terminal disclaimer cannot be used to overcome a 102(e)/103(a) rejection. For commonly owned references, consider 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(1) disqualification rules and other procedural options (co-filing, merging, affidavits under 37 CFR 1.132 or declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 where applicable) as alternatives to invoking prior art effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling commonly-owned references and disqualification under 35 U.S.C. 103(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: For applications filed on/after Nov 29, 1999 and pending on/after Dec 10, 2004, a commonly assigned/owned patent or application may be disqualified as 102(e) prior art in a 103(a) rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatives to invoking 103(c)(1) include filing applications on the same day, merging copending apps into a CIP and abandoning parents, or using 37 CFR 1.132 and 1.131 affidavits/declarations to show derivation or earlier invention dates. For post-Dec 10, 2004 pendency, be mindful of joint research agreement provisions (103(c)(2)/(3)) and the evidentiary requirements to disqualify references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make both double patenting and 102/103 rejections when supported
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner should make both a 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103(a) rejection and a double patenting rejection over the same reference when the facts support both rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If each rejection is separately applicable but the examiner includes only one, then adding the omitted rejection in the next office action prevents making that next action final. For applications pending on/after Dec 10, 2004, rejections under 102(e)/103(a) should not be made or maintained if the reference is disqualified under 103(c) as prior art in a 103(a) rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to establish joint research agreement before applying related double patenting rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Until applicant establishes the existence of a joint research agreement, the examiner cannot apply a double patenting rejection based on the possible existence of such an agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant disqualifies a relied-upon reference under 103(c) in reply to a 102/103 rejection, and a subsequent double patenting rejection based on the disqualified reference is applied, the next Office action may be made final (provided no other new grounds appear) because the new double patenting rejection was necessitated by applicant’s amendment or filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 121 prohibition on double patenting rejections in restriction/divisional contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 121 prohibits use of a patent issuing on an application subject to a restriction requirement as a reference against any divisional application if the divisional is filed before the patent issues, but only where the Office made a requirement for restriction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies where claims in each application were filed as a result of an Office restriction requirement (e.g., combination vs subcombination, process vs apparatus, etc.). The Office must guard against erroneous restriction requirements. The prohibition does not apply where the divisional was voluntarily filed, where claims are not consonant with the restriction, where requirements were withdrawn, or other enumerated exceptions (see next rubric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to 35 U.S.C. 121 prohibition (A–G)
rubrics_metrics.description: Situations where the 35 U.S.C. 121 prohibition does not apply: (A) applicant voluntarily filed multiple applications without an examiner restriction; (B) claims are not consonant with restriction because materially changed; (C) restriction was made subject to nonallowance of generic/linking claims and such claims later allowed; (D) restriction made only in an international application by ISA/IPEA; (E) restriction withdrawn before patent issues; (F) claims of second application are drawn to the 'same invention' as the first; (G) where a restriction was made subject to nonallowance of product and product subsequently allowed, requiring withdrawal of restriction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain the line of demarcation between independent and distinct inventions identified in the restriction requirement for consonance. Note that continuation practice where restriction not reinstated may allow reliance on continuity despite earlier restriction language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding statutory double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory double patenting can be avoided by amending conflicting claims so they are not coextensive in scope, canceling conflicting claims in pending applications, or cancelling conflicting claims in all but one pending application for provisional rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminal disclaimers are not effective against statutory double patenting. Use of 37 CFR 1.131 affidavits is inappropriate for statutory double patenting (case law: In re Dunn and progeny).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding nonstatutory double patenting (terminal disclaimer guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonstatutory double patenting rejection can be obviated by filing a terminal disclaimer in the application or proceeding in which the rejection is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminal disclaimers encourage disclosure and earlier filing; filing is not an admission of the rejection's propriety. Terminal disclaimer must operate with respect to all claims in the patent (cannot disclaim term of only specified claims). Where subject matter was commonly owned at the time of invention, disclaimers must include a provision making the patent unenforceable if it ceases to be commonly owned (37 CFR 1.321(c)). Terminal disclaimers cannot overcome 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103(a) rejections. 37 CFR 1.131 affidavits are inappropriate to overcome nonstatutory double patenting when claims are substantially the same or lack patentable distinctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer formal requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements for a terminal disclaimer are set forth in 37 CFR 1.321; sample forms and filing/treatment guidance are in MPEP § 1490.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A terminal disclaimer is a statement filed by an owner to disclaim or dedicate a portion of the entire term of all claims of a patent. Ensure compliance with 37 CFR 1.321 provisions, including special provisions for common ownership and joint research agreements (1.321(c) and (d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory terminal disclaimer for continuing applications filed on/after June 8, 1995
rubrics_metrics.description: For continuing utility or plant applications filed on/after June 8, 1995, a terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321 is required to overcome a nonstatutory double patenting rejection, even if the continuing application claims benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, or 365(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: 35 U.S.C. 154(a)(2) provides a 20-year term from earliest claimed filing date, and 154(b) allows term adjustments; to avoid potential term-extension problems and harassment by multiple owners, the terminal disclaimer must include provisions required by 37 CFR 1.321(c)(3) and (d) as applicable. Cite MPEP section or Official Gazette notice when responding to arguments that 37 CFR 1.321 should not be required due to 35 U.S.C. 154.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling multiple conflicting double patenting references in terminal disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: If multiple conflicting patents and/or pending applications are applied in double patenting rejections in a single application, it is necessary prior to issuance to disclaim the terminal part of any patent granted on the application which would extend beyond the application date of each conflicting patent/application, or file a single terminal disclaimer based on common ownership including all conflicting references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A terminal disclaimer fee is required for each disclaimer filed; to avoid multiple fees, a single common-ownership disclaimer may be filed covering all conflicting commonly owned references. Each commonly owned conflicting reference must be included to avoid dual-ownership problems if ownership ceases to be common. For joint research agreements, follow 37 CFR 1.321(d) requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional double patenting practice across multiple pending applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a provisional double patenting rejection is made in one of two or more pending applications, the examiner should follow practice in MPEP § 804 subsection I.B.1 to determine in which application an appropriate terminal disclaimer must be filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional rejections should also be made in conflicting applications; claims that differ aside from minor language differences are not considered the same invention, but if differences would have been obvious, terminal disclaimers are effective. Ensure consistency of provisional rejections across related files and coordinate terminal disclaimer filing as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inapplicability of 37 CFR 1.131 affidavits to overcome double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit (or similar) is inappropriate to overcome either statutory or nonstatutory double patenting rejections when the claims are directed to substantially the same invention or lack patentable distinctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (In re Dunn, Knell v. Muller, and related CCPA decisions) supports that 1.131 is inapplicable where the application claims and the patent claim the same or substantially the same invention. Instead, rely on claim amendments, cancellations, or terminal disclaimers (for nonstatutory) as appropriate.
